Eswatini National Family Planning Services Guidelines (2021): re-extracted tables, boxes and flowcharts

Every table in FP guideline pages 1-67 (part 1), read from the PDF page image by Claude: merged cells, section rows and footnotes kept for tables; branches, combined conditions and line breaks kept for flowcharts, with their captions and printed notes folded in. Compare each with the page on the left. "Points to check in the source" lists problems in the guideline itself. The "what the model receives" version fills merged cells in, shows a long note that spans every row once, and attaches footnotes. The embedding text is split into parts under 512 tokens that all return the whole table.

Abstinence: Advantages and disadvantages (Advantages, Disadvantages)
AdvantagesDisadvantages
• Encourages partner’s communication on contraception<br/>• Abstinence has no side effects<br/>• It is supported by religious beliefs and socio-cultural norms.<br/>• Delays sexual debut for the adolescents and young people<br/>• Provides 100% protection against pregnancy and reduces risk of sexually transmitted infections and HIV.• Both partners must decide, agree and be fully committed to use abstinence.<br/>• It requires self-control<br/>• It can have a high failure rate, especially if drugs and alcohol are used.

Fertility Awareness Methods: Advantages and disadvantages (Advantages, Disadvantages)
AdvantagesDisadvantages
• Fertility Awareness methods have no side effects.<br/>• Improve knowledge of the reproductive system and understanding of menstrual cycle.<br/>• Shared responsibility by partners.<br/>• Less expensive.<br/>• Do not require procedures and usually do not require supplies<br/>• Limited need for professional consultation.<br/>• Allows some partners to adhere to their religious or cultural norms<br/>• Can assist partners in achieving a wanted pregnancy.<br/>• Return to fertility is immediate.• No protection against sexually transmitted infections including HIV<br/>• Need cooperation and commitment by both partners.<br/>• Require intensive education and instruction before being confident to use method.<br/>• May not be easy to use if menstrual cycle is irregular.<br/>• Require accurate record keeping.<br/>• Unreliable if client is breastfeeding and has amenorrhea.<br/>• Has a high failure rate if client is not well trained and there is no commitment and cooperation between partners.

When to Start (Woman’s situation, Symptoms Based Methods, Calendar Method)

New: table with merged cells (as in the PDF)

When to Start (Woman’s situation, Symptoms Based Methods, Calendar Method)
Woman’s situationSymptoms Based MethodsCalendar Method
Regular menstrual cycles• Any time of the month.<br/>• No need to wait until the start of next monthly bleeding• Any time of the month<br/>• No need to wait until the start of next monthly bleeding.
Amenorrhoea• Delay until menses return• Delay until menses return
After childbirth (whether or not breastfeeding)• She can start symptoms-based methods once normal vaginal secretions have returned.<br/>• Normal vaginal secretions will return later in breastfeeding women than in women who are not breastfeeding.• Delay the method until she has had 3-6 menstrual cycles, and the last one was 26 to 32 days long<br/>• Regular cycles will return later in breastfeeding women than in women who are not breastfeeding
After miscarriage or abortion• She can start immediately with special counselling and support, if she has no infection-related secretions or bleeding due to injury to the genital tract.• Delay until the start of her next monthly period, if she has no infection-related secretions or bleeding due to injury to the genital tract.
Switching from a hormonal method• She can start symptoms-based methods in the next menstrual cycle after stopping a hormonal method. Use of condom is encouraged while waiting for the next menstrual cycle.• Delay starting the Standard Days Method until the start of her next monthly bleeding.<br/>• If she is switching from injectables, delay the Standard Days Method at least until her repeat injection would have been due, and then start it at the beginning of her next monthly bleeding
After taking emergency contraceptive pills• She can start symptoms-based methods once normal secretions have returned.• Delay the Standard Days Method until the start of her next monthly bleeding.

Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM): Advantages and disadvantages (Advantages, Disadvantages)
AdvantagesDisadvantages
• Is universally available and free.<br/>• Helps protect against the risk of<br/>pregnancy<br/>• Encourages exclusive<br/>breastfeeding.<br/>• It does not interfere with the act<br/>of sexual intercourse.<br/>• No supplies or procedures<br/>needed and has no side effects.<br/>• Effective in all women<br/>regardless of body weight• Provides no protection against<br/>STI’s including HIV.<br/>• Effectiveness after exclusive<br/>breastfeeding period is not certain.<br/>• Frequent breastfeeding may<br/>be inconvenient or difficult for<br/>some women, especially working<br/>mothers.<br/>• If the mother is HIV positive there<br/>is a risk that the virus will be<br/>transmitted to the baby through the<br/>breast milk.<br/>• If woman develops severe medical<br/>breasts conditions, the method can<br/>be compromised.

Coitus Interruptus: Advantages and disadvantages (Advantages, Disadvantages)
AdvantagesDisadvantages

When a pill or more is missed (Number of Missed Pills, Action to be taken)

PDF page 38 · fp-2021-tbl-p38-0058 · replaces fp-2021-0058
All numbers match (compared with the PDF text layer and the old chunks)
Points to check in the source:
  • Missed progestin-only pills: the instructions ('take 2 pills as soon as she can and another 2 the next day'; for 3 missed pills 'do not attempt to replace') are combined-pill style. For POPs, WHO advises taking one pill as soon as possible whenever a pill is more than 3 hours late (27 hours for desogestrel), continuing daily, and using a backup method for the next 2 days.

PDF page

New: table with merged cells (as in the PDF)

When a pill or more is missed (Number of Missed Pills, Action to be taken)
Number of Missed PillsAction to be taken
1 pillShe should take the pill as soon as she can then continue at the usual time. Use a backup method for 2 days after the missed pill.
2 pillsShe should take 2 pills as soon as she can and take another 2 pills the next day then return to her regular schedule on the 3rd day. A backup method of contraception should be used.
3 pillsDo not attempt to replace as above; She should use a backup method of contraception and report to the health facility for professional help as soon as possible.

Progesterone-Only Oral Pills (pops): Advantages and disadvantages of POPs (Advantages, Disadvantages)

Progesterone-Only Oral Pills (pops): Advantages and disadvantages of POPs (Advantages, Disadvantages)
AdvantagesDisadvantages
• Can be used during breastfeeding anytime between giving birth and 6 months<br/>• Do not affect breast milk production.<br/>• Suitable for women with risk factors such as heart attack, stroke and thrombosis.<br/>• Less side effects such as acne and weight gain.<br/>• Return to fertility is immediate upon discontinuation.<br/>• Non contraceptive health benefits which include prevention of endometrial cancer, and anaemia.• Do not protect against STIs including HIV and AIDS<br/>• They require strict daily pill-taking, preferably at the same time each day<br/>• Irregular bleeding and spotting is common<br/>• Less effective in women who are not breastfeeding<br/>• Effectiveness may decrease if clients are also taking some other medications (anti-TB drugs, anticonvulsants and antiretroviral (Retinovir boosted and NNRTI based, etc) so a client should use a backup method or change the medication/ method altogether.<br/>• Effectiveness may also be lowered in the presence of diarrhoea and vomiting

New: what the model receives

Progesterone-Only Oral Pills (pops): Advantages and disadvantages of POPs (Advantages, Disadvantages)

Advantages and disadvantages of POPs

AdvantagesDisadvantages
• Can be used during breastfeeding anytime between giving birth and 6 months
• Do not affect breast milk production.
• Suitable for women with risk factors such as heart attack, stroke and thrombosis.
• Less side effects such as acne and weight gain.
• Return to fertility is immediate upon discontinuation.
• Non contraceptive health benefits which include prevention of endometrial cancer, and anaemia.		• Do not protect against STIs including HIV and AIDS
• They require strict daily pill-taking, preferably at the same time each day
• Irregular bleeding and spotting is common
• Less effective in women who are not breastfeeding
• Effectiveness may decrease if clients are also taking some other medications (anti-TB drugs, anticonvulsants and antiretroviral (Retinovir boosted and NNRTI based, etc) so a client should use a backup method or change the medication/ method altogether.
• Effectiveness may also be lowered in the presence of diarrhoea and vomiting

  • POP eligibility categories differ from the WHO MEC: elevated BP ≥160/100, history of DVT, stroke and ischaemic heart disease at initiation are WHO category 2 for POPs (here 3); acute DVT/PE, ischaemic heart disease or stroke while continuing, and SLE with antiphospholipid antibodies are WHO category 3 (here 4).

PROGESTON-ONLY INJECTABLE CONTRACEPTIVES (POIs): Advantages and disadvantages of POIs (Advantages, Disadvantages)
AdvantagesDisadvantages
• Can be used during breastfeeding starting after childbirth<br/>• Do not affect breast milk production<br/>• Suitable for women with risk factors such as heart attack, stroke and thrombosis.<br/>• Provides highly effective protection against pregnancy.<br/>• Ensures periodic contact with medical or trained health personnel.<br/>• Only requires to remember the clinic return dates<br/>• It can be confidential: no one else can tell that a woman is using contraception<br/>• Non-contraceptive health benefits which include prevention of endometrial cancer, uterine fibroids, endometrial cancers, Pelvic Inflammatory Diseases, endometriosis and anaemia.<br/>• Decreases incidence of pre-menstrual or postmenstrual depression and epileptic seizures<br/>• Do not make a woman infertile and do not disrupt an existing pregnancy• Do not protect against STIs including HIV and AIDS<br/>• May cause changes in menstrual bleeding patterns.<br/>• May cause indirect weight changes and acne.<br/>• Requires repeat injection every 2 or 3 months.<br/>• There may be delayed return to fertility and cannot be reversed immediately.<br/>• May cause headaches, breast tenderness, nausea, hair loss, reduced and changes in libido

PROGESTON-ONLY INJECTABLE CONTRACEPTIVES (POIs): Advantages and disadvantages of POIs (Advantages, Disadvantages)

Advantages and disadvantages of POIs

AdvantagesDisadvantages
• Can be used during breastfeeding starting after childbirth
• Do not affect breast milk production
• Suitable for women with risk factors such as heart attack, stroke and thrombosis.
• Provides highly effective protection against pregnancy.
• Ensures periodic contact with medical or trained health personnel.
• Only requires to remember the clinic return dates
• It can be confidential: no one else can tell that a woman is using contraception
• Non-contraceptive health benefits which include prevention of endometrial cancer, uterine fibroids, endometrial cancers, Pelvic Inflammatory Diseases, endometriosis and anaemia.
• Decreases incidence of pre-menstrual or postmenstrual depression and epileptic seizures
• Do not make a woman infertile and do not disrupt an existing pregnancy		• Do not protect against STIs including HIV and AIDS
• May cause changes in menstrual bleeding patterns.
• May cause indirect weight changes and acne.
• Requires repeat injection every 2 or 3 months.
• There may be delayed return to fertility and cannot be reversed immediately.
• May cause headaches, breast tenderness, nausea, hair loss, reduced and changes in libido

Combined Oral Contraceptives (COCs): Advantages and disadvantages of using COCs (Advantages, Disadvantages)
AdvantagesDisadvantages
• Easy to use<br/>• Can be used from adolescence to menopause; by nulliparous and multiparous women; provided that no risk factors exist.<br/>Help protect against:<br/>• Risks of pregnancy<br/>• Cancer of the lining of the uterus (endometrial cancer)<br/>• Cancer of the ovary<br/>• Symptomatic pelvic inflammatory disease<br/>• Ovarian cysts<br/>• Iron-deficiency anaemia<br/>• Reduce menstrual cramps<br/>• Supresses menstrual bleeding problems<br/>• Reduce ovulation pain<br/>• Reduce excess hair on face or body<br/>• Minimises symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (irregular period, acne, excess hair on face or body)<br/>• Reduce symptoms of endometriosis (pelvic pain, irregular bleeding)• Does not protect against STIs and HIV infection.<br/>• Must be taken daily and at the same time<br/>• Require an individual to obtain regular supplies.<br/>• Effectiveness may be lowered if client is on anti-TB drugs (Rifampicin or Rifabutin therapy), anti-epilepsy treatment and some ARVs indicating a need for a backup method.<br/>• Effectiveness may also be lowered in the presence of diarrhoea and vomiting<br/>• Reduce milk production in breastfeeding women.<br/>• May cause mood changes and low libido to some women<br/>• Can increase the risk of Myocardial Infarction (MI) in women with existing risk factors such as smoking, Diabetes or hypertension.

New: what the model receives

Combined Oral Contraceptives (COCs): Advantages and disadvantages of using COCs (Advantages, Disadvantages)

Advantages and disadvantages of using COCs

AdvantagesDisadvantages
• Easy to use
• Can be used from adolescence to menopause; by nulliparous and multiparous women; provided that no risk factors exist.
Help protect against:
• Risks of pregnancy
• Cancer of the lining of the uterus (endometrial cancer)
• Cancer of the ovary
• Symptomatic pelvic inflammatory disease
• Ovarian cysts
• Iron-deficiency anaemia
• Reduce menstrual cramps
• Supresses menstrual bleeding problems
• Reduce ovulation pain
• Reduce excess hair on face or body
• Minimises symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (irregular period, acne, excess hair on face or body)
• Reduce symptoms of endometriosis (pelvic pain, irregular bleeding)		• Does not protect against STIs and HIV infection.
• Must be taken daily and at the same time
• Require an individual to obtain regular supplies.
• Effectiveness may be lowered if client is on anti-TB drugs (Rifampicin or Rifabutin therapy), anti-epilepsy treatment and some ARVs indicating a need for a backup method.
• Effectiveness may also be lowered in the presence of diarrhoea and vomiting
• Reduce milk production in breastfeeding women.
• May cause mood changes and low libido to some women
• Can increase the risk of Myocardial Infarction (MI) in women with existing risk factors such as smoking, Diabetes or hypertension.

MEC Category 1MEC Category 2MEC Category 3MEC Category 4
Nearly all women can use COCs safely and effectively, including women who:

• Have anemia now or had in the past
• Have varicose veins
• Are living with HIV, whether or not on antiretroviral therapy		• Age above 40 years
• Breastfeeding more than 6 months after delivery
• Non-breastfeeding women 21 – 42 days with no risk of venous thromboembolism
• Smoking and age less than 35 years
• Obesity
• History of p high blood pressure during pregnancy
• Family history of DVT/PE
• Major surgery without prolonged immobilization
• Superficial thrombophlebitis
• Uncomplicated Valvular heart disease • Systemic lupus erythematous (associated with severe thrombocytopenia or are on Immunosuppressive treatment)
• Non-migraine headache (mild or severe) in continuing clients
• Migraine headache without aura at age less than 35 years for Initiating clients
• Unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation
• Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia or cervical cancer awaiting treatment
• Undiagnosed breast mass
• Insulin dependent Diabetes Mellitus
• Asymptomatic gall bladder disease
• HIV treatment with NNRTIs and PIs		• Breastfeeding 6 weeks to 6 months after delivery
• Acute Viral hepatitis
• TB patients on Rifampicin or Rifabutin therapy
• Anticonvulsant therapy (phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates)		• Breastfeeding less than 6 weeks postpartum
• Smoking and age more than 35 year (smoking more than 15 cigarettes/day)
• Non-breastfeeding less than 21 days after delivery with or without risk of venous thromboembolism
• Symptomatic gall bladder disease (medically treated and current)
• Severe hypertension (systolic >160 or diastolic >100 mm Hg) and hypertension with vascular complications
• Hypertension (history of hypertension, hypertension controlled on treatment, moderate hypertension) • History of DVT/PE or current DVT/PE or DVT/PE on anticoagulant therapy
• Major surgery with prolonged immobilization
• History of stroke
• History of or current ischaemic heart disease
• Complicated Valvular heart disease
• Systemic Lupus Erythematosus with positive antiphospholipid antibodies
• Migraine headache with aura at any age
• Severe liver cirrhosis (decompensated)
• Current breast cancer
• Liver Cancer
• Known thrombogenic mutation
• Benign liver tumours

• Current breast cancer
• Liver Cancer
• Known thrombogenic mutation
• Benign liver tumours

Combined Injectable Contraceptives (CICs): Advantages and disadvantages (Advantages, Disadvantages)
AdvantagesDisadvantages
• Do not require daily action<br/>• Are private:<br/>No one else can tell that a woman is using contraception<br/>• Can be stopped at any time<br/>• Are good for spacing births• Does not protect against STIs and HIV infection.<br/>• Requires injection monthly<br/>• Must be administered by a trained health service provider.<br/>• Effectiveness may be lowered if client is on anti-TB drugs (Rifampicin or Rifabutin therapy), anti-epilepsy treatment and some ARVs etc., indicating a need for a backup method.<br/>• Cannot be given to breastfeeding women with babies less than six months. Implants: Advantages and disadvantages (Advantages, Disadvantages)
AdvantagesDisadvantages
• Provide long-term pregnancy protection.<br/>• Do not require the user to do anything once<br/>they are inserted<br/>• Are both long-lasting and reversible<br/>• Do not interfere with sex<br/>• Very effective for 3 to 5 years, depending on<br/>the type of implant used.<br/>• Immediately reversible.<br/>• Avoids user errors and problems with<br/>resupply<br/>• Helps protect against symptomatic pelvic<br/>inflammatory disease (PID)<br/>• Reduces risk of ectopic pregnancies<br/>• Cut down menstrual pains• Does not protect<br/>against STIs and HIV/<br/>AIDS<br/>• Require specifically<br/>trained provider to<br/>insert and remove.<br/>• A woman cannot start<br/>or stop implants on her<br/>own.
